Where it began

Salman Butt was born in Lahore on 7 October 1984 and went to school in the Beaconhouse system. He came up quickly. After the Under-17 and Under-19 sides Lahore Whites gave him his first senior game in 2000, when he was only 15, and soon found himself in a Pakistan A team facing England.

Rather than being hurried into the national side, he spent a few seasons building his game with his region and the youth teams. The call finally came in 2003.

The player

His first Test was against Bangladesh in September 2003. He played 33 Tests for Pakistan, the last in 2010, and made 1,889 runs at 30.47, with three hundreds, 10 fifties and a highest score of 122. He was a regular at the top of the order in both Tests and one-day games.

The early years were a scramble for a place among plenty of good openers. Things settled during a winter series against England, when he made a hundred and two fifties with a more patient approach than before. In 2010 he was named Test captain, the 28th man to lead Pakistan, and his first match in charge, against Australia, ended in victory. He was also in the squad that won the 2009 World Twenty20.

What made him special

He was a craftsman rather than a hitter. Most of his runs went between backward point and extra cover, steered into the gaps with supple wrists and the bowler's own pace. Against spin, with no slips in place, he loved to cut fine down to third man. He hit only six sixes in his Test career, which made each one feel like an occasion.

India seemed to bring out the best in him. In one-day games against them he made five hundreds in 21 innings. The finest may have been in November 2004, when Pakistan chased 292. Laid low by cramp, he left the field for seven overs, then came back to finish the job with 108 not out.

Commentators sometimes felt he was tempted by balls outside off stump that were better left alone. It is a fair point, and one most openers would recognise.

Away from the middle

He kept scoring runs in domestic cricket for years. Playing for WAPDA he made a hundred in each innings of a Quaid-e-Azam Trophy final, and with Kamran Akmal he shared an unbeaten opening stand of 209 in a domestic Twenty20 match, then the highest opening partnership in any T20 cricket. The one-day Quaid-e-Azam competition of 2018–19 ended with nobody ahead of him on the run-scoring list.

Later he took a course in umpiring and refereeing, and in 2022 became a consultant coach to the Singapore national side.

And finally

For a batsman who rarely bothered the crowd in the stands, he got through a remarkable amount of work behind square on the off side.
